data.walkthrough#Walkthrough:
Most setups are one of these two. Follow the one that matches how the image is built.
One application, with the Dockerfile in a hosted repository: A single service built from Git. Several services built from a Compose project on disk, plus containers that should stay on the registry: A Compose project on disk. Starting Watchtower does not rebuild the application. An update session does, and only after the hosted ref moves past the revision Watchtower already knows.
You need the Docker socket mounted into Watchtower. A private repository needs a read token in a Docker Secret. Do not put the token in the compose file, and do not put the raw token in the process environment.
data.watcher-precedence#Watcher Precedence: com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-watch Git Enable Watcher absent false off absent true on enabling value either on disabling value either off
data.what-git-monitoring-does#What Git Monito:
Git monitoring is an alternate staleness signal. It does not replace registry digest checks for containers that are not associated with a repository. The Watchtower container itself always stays on the registry self-update path.
Stage What Watchtower does Git monitoring Talks to the hosted remote and compares the configured branch or tag to the known running revision Image build Asks the Docker host, or Compose, to rebuild from the chosen build context Container update Recreates the container from inspect config, or applies Compose for a local path context
data.what-git-monitoring-does-not-do#What Git: It does not Use this instead Watch a local working tree for file saves Compose Watch Rebuild because a stamp label is missing Wait until the hosted ref advances Invent Compose or run configuration Put that configuration on the container or in the Compose project Treat org.opencontainers.image.source as an association Set com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-repo or Git Image See Local filesystem monitoring.
data.what-happens-in-a-session#What Happens i:
For each associated container whose watcher is on:
Resolve the repository URL, ref, and semver policy from labels or the Git Image configuration option. Check the hosted remote for the current branch tip or a policy-allowed tag. Compare that tip to the known running revision. If the remote has not advanced, leave the running container untouched. If the remote has advanced, rebuild from the chosen build context. After a successful rebuild, write stamp labels on the replacement. Annotated tags are resolved to the peeled commit, not the tag object.
data.what-is-written-after-a-rebuild#What Is:
A rebuilt container, whether Watchtower recreated it or Compose applied it, carries the association labels it needs on its next check.
com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-repo is written without credentials. com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-host is written as the API origin, without credentials or a query. com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-ref, com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-semver-policy, com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-dockerfile, and com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-context are written only when a label or a Git Image mapping supplied them. Values that came from the Git Dockerfile or Git Context configuration options are not written. A later change to those options still applies to the rebuilt container. The built-in defaults, the main ref and the none semver policy, are not written either. git-watch=true is written only when the source container already had an explicit enabling watch label. When the watcher was on only because of the Git Enable configuration option, the replacement has no git-watch label. Setting Git Enable to false later still applies.
Containers rebuilt through Compose by v1.24.0 or earlier Those releases also wrote the default ref, semver policy, Dockerfile, and context onto containers rebuilt through Compose. A container rebuilt that way treats them as its own labels. A later change to Git Dockerfile or Git Context does not reach it. To check a container, run docker inspect -f '{{json .Config.Labels}}' CONTAINER and look for com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-dockerfile and com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-context. Replace CONTAINER with the container name. If you did not set them, recreate the container with docker compose up -d --force-recreate SERVICE so it starts from the labels in your Compose file. Replace SERVICE with the container’s Compose service.
data.what-the-daemon-builds#What the Daemon B:
On a stale session:
Watchtower builds a Docker Git URL context: https://git.example.com/org/app.git#COMMIT, or #COMMIT:SUBDIRECTORY when com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-context or the Git Context configuration option is set. Here COMMIT is the commit to build and SUBDIRECTORY is the build context directory. The Docker daemon (BuildKit) performs a shallow clone of that commit. Watchtower does not clone the tree first. The Dockerfile is com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-dockerfile, or the Git Dockerfile configuration option, defaulting to Dockerfile. Watchtower tags the image with its original name and with NAME:git-SHORT_SHA, where SHORT_SHA is the commit’s first 12 hex characters. Watchtower recreates the container from the running inspect config. Stamp labels are written onto the new container.
data.what-to-put-in-it#What to Put In It: The API base URL only, for example https://git.example.com:3000 or https://git.example.com/gitlab. Do not include a repository path. For an unknown self-hosted hostname, only the exact single-segment prefixes github, gitlab, gitea, forgejo, and codeberg provide a provider hint for changelog derivation. A pathless or custom multi-segment prefix does not identify the provider.
data.what-watchtower-applies#What Watchtower:
On a stale session:
Group stale, associated containers that share the same resolved project directory. Fetch the hosted remote in that directory once per project. Check out the monitored commit. Apply Compose for the stale associated service names only. Write stamp and association labels onto the new containers. Do not also recreate those containers through the inspect path. Every stale service in that directory must resolve the same commit. One worktree cannot be checked out at two commits. When the commits differ, Watchtower leaves the project untouched and retries on a later session.
Compose uses each service’s build.context relative to the project directory. Image-only services in the same file are not rebuilt from Git.
Jobs in the Compose file are left out of the apply. Watchtower does not register or compare them, so a scheduled job keeps the definition your own docker compose up registered. An apply also works when the engine’s jobs extension is off. To register a changed job, follow Compose’s steps for changing a registered job .
Fetch uses the same Git Auth Token, Git Password, Git SSH Key Path, Git CA Bundle, and Git Insecure Skip TLS configuration options as monitoring. If fetch fails but the monitored commit is already in the local object store, checkout continues.
data.when-a-container-uses-the-git-path#When:
Both of the following must be true:
The container is associated with a repository, using com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-repo or the Git Image configuration option. The Git watcher is on, using the Git Enable configuration option or com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-watch. com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-repo does not replace the Label Enable configuration option.
data.when-to-use-it#When to Use It:
Use this when the image should be built from a hosted Git URL, the same as Compose build.context: https://host/repo.git.
Typical setup: a single service whose image tracks https://git.example.com/org/app.git on main or a tag policy. The Dockerfile lives in that repository.
A Git URL context does not read compose.yaml. New env vars, services, or volumes added only in Compose are not applied. Use a local path context when the compose file is the source of truth.
data.when-to-use-it-1#When to Use It:
Use this when the running services were created from a Compose file that uses a local build.context (build: ./api), and you mount that Compose project directory into Watchtower.
Typical setup: api and worker with build: ./api or build: ./worker, plus image-only dependencies that stay on the registry path.
A Compose build: key alone does not associate a container. The container still needs a Git association and the watcher to be on.
data.when-you-do-not-need-it#When You Do Not: The repository is on github.com, gitlab.com, or codeberg.org The clone URL is already https://git.example.com/org/app.git on port 443 and you only need Watchtower to ask Git
data.when-you-need-it#When You Need It:
The container’s git-repo is an SSH URL, or the HTTP API is on a different port or path than the clone URL, and you want Watchtower to use that HTTP API.
The label’s hostname must match the clone URL. git@git.example.com:org/app.git may use https://git.example.com:3000. A different hostname is ignored, and Watchtower asks Git on the clone URL. The process token is not sent to that other host.
data.where-settings-come-from#Where Settings:
Watchtower reads the repository URL, ref, and semver policy from the container’s Watchtower labels when com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-repo is set.
If that label is absent, Watchtower uses the Git Image mapping whose key matches the container’s exact ImageName(). There is no process-wide default repository.
Container labelsGit Image mappingLabels and a mapping Use this when the Git settings belong on the service itself.
Docker ComposeDocker CLI services: app: image: myapp:latest labels: com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-repo: "https://github.com/org/app.git" com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-ref: "main" com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-semver-policy: "minor" docker run -d \ --name app \ --label com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-repo="https://github.com/org/app.git" \ --label com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-ref="main" \ --label com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-semver-policy="minor" \ myapp:latest Watchtower uses https://github.com/org/app.git on main with a minor semver policy.
Use the Git Image configuration option when you do not want Git labels on every service. The mapping key must match ImageName() including the tag (app is not app:latest). The mapping does not turn the watcher on.
Docker ComposeDocker CLI services: watchtower: image: nickfedor/watchtower volumes: - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock environment: WATCHTOWER_GIT_ENABLE: "true" WATCHTOWER_GIT_IMAGE: | myapp:latest=https://github.com/org/app.git#main@minor app: image: myapp:latest docker run -d \ --name app \ myapp:latest docker run -d \ --name watchtower \ -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \ --restart unless-stopped \ -e WATCHTOWER_GIT_ENABLE=true \ -e WATCHTOWER_GIT_IMAGE="myapp:latest=https://github.com/org/app.git#main@minor" \ nickfedor/watchtower app has no Git labels. Watchtower uses the mapping for myapp:latest: https://github.com/org/app.git on main with a minor semver policy.
When both are present, the container labels are used. The Git Image mapping is ignored for that container.
Docker ComposeDocker CLI services: watchtower: image: nickfedor/watchtower volumes: - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock environment: WATCHTOWER_GIT_ENABLE: "true" WATCHTOWER_GIT_IMAGE: | myapp:latest=https://github.com/org/app.git#develop@major app: image: myapp:latest labels: com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-repo: "https://github.com/org/app.git" com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-ref: "main" com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-semver-policy: "patch" docker run -d \ --name app \ --label com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-repo="https://github.com/org/app.git" \ --label com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-ref="main" \ --label com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-semver-policy="patch" \ myapp:latest docker run -d \ --name watchtower \ -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \ --restart unless-stopped \ -e WATCHTOWER_GIT_ENABLE=true \ -e WATCHTOWER_GIT_IMAGE="myapp:latest=https://github.com/org/app.git#develop@major" \ nickfedor/watchtower Watchtower uses main and patch from the labels, not develop and major from the mapping.

data: The image cooldown feature enforces a configurable minimum image age before Watchtower will apply an update to a container. By requiring that an image has existed in the registry for a certain period of time, the cooldown provides a defense against supply-chain attacks, where a compromised image is published and immediately pulled by automated update tools. In addition, this helps to reduce the chance of receiving potentially buggy updates prior to the developer releasing an emergency patch.
data.anonymous-and-authenticated-checks#Anony: AnonymousAuthenticated One anonymous token is reused across public images, and later images in that token lifetime skip the registry challenge. Checks run one at a time so parallel requests cannot drain the shared bucket in a burst. Every request draws from the org’s shared bucket. docker login ghcr.io, or equivalent credentials in config.json or REPO_USER and REPO_PASS, separates your checks from anonymous throttling and restores parallel checks. Pulls of a public org can still land in that org’s shared bucket, so credentials reduce but do not remove top-of-the-hour throttling. Login to lscr.io alone does not count. Credential lookup uses ghcr.io after the remap.
data.docker-hub#Docker Hub:
Official Documentation: https://docs.docker.com/docker-hub/usage/pulls/ Docker Hub enforces pull rate limits per six-hour window:
Account Type Pull Limit Unauthenticated 100 pulls per IP (IPv4) or /64 subnet (IPv6) Personal (free, authenticated) 200 pulls Pro / Team / Business Unlimited Not all registry requests count as pulls. Verified behavior (tested against nickfedor/watchtower on Docker Hub):
Request Type Counts as Pull? HEAD manifest No GET manifest Yes GET config blob (307 → CDN) No Auth token request No The existing digest comparison uses a HEAD request, which does not consume a pull. The cooldown age check uses GET requests for manifests, which do consume pulls, but the config blob fetch is served via a CDN redirect (307) and does not count against the limit.
data.duration-format#Duration Format:
Cooldown values are specified as a duration string. The following units are supported:
Unit Description Example s Seconds 90s m Minutes 30m h Hours 24h d Days 3d w Weeks 1w M Months 1M Units can be combined:
24h — 24 hours 3d12h — 3 days and 12 hours 1w — 7 days 1M — 30 days (approximate)
data.examples#Examples: Docker ComposeDocker CLI services: watchtower: image: nickfedor/watchtower volumes: - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock environment: - WATCHTOWER_COOLDOWN_DELAY=24h # Inherits the global 24h cooldown web: image: nginx:latest ports: - "80:80" # Override: requires image to be 48 hours old api: image: myorg/api:latest ports: - "8080:8080" labels: - "com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.cooldown-delay=48h" # Override: cooldown disabled — update immediately redis: image: redis:latest labels: - "com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.cooldown-delay=0" docker run -d \ --name watchtower \ -e WATCHTOWER_COOLDOWN_DELAY=24h \ -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \ nickfedor/watchtower docker run -d \ --name myapp \ --label=com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.cooldown-delay="72h" \ myorg/myapp:latest
data.github-container-registry-ghcrio#GitHub:
GHCR does not publish Docker Hub-style pull quotas. Requests for a public org’s packages draw from one undocumented token bucket per org, observed as allowed: 44000/minute with a sub-millisecond retry-after. The same bucket serves lscr.io/linuxserver/* images, which Watchtower remaps to ghcr.io for digest checks and authentication.
Shared org buckets run dry at the top of every hour Buckets for popular orgs such as linuxserver are observed empty for the first one to two minutes of each hour, when scheduled update tools fire together. A run that starts at :00 sends its first pulls into that window. See Scheduling Around the Hour.
data.global-configuration#Global Configuratio:
Set the cooldown delay for all monitored containers using the cooldown-delay configuration option.
Docker ComposeDocker CLIDockerfile services: watchtower: image: nickfedor/watchtower volumes: - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock environment: - WATCHTOWER_COOLDOWN_DELAY=24h docker run -d \ --name watchtower \ -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \ --restart unless-stopped \ nickfedor/watchtower \ --cooldown-delay 24h ... WATCHTOWER_COOLDOWN_DELAY=24h ...
data.handling-a-429-response#Handling a 429 R:
Watchtower reads the retry-after value of a 429 response and handles it in one of three ways:
retry-after Meaning Watchtower response Below 100ms The shared bucket is empty right now Ignores the value and backs off exponentially from 100ms toward 30 seconds, for up to 3 minutes from the first throttle 100ms to 30 seconds A wait the registry asked for Honors the wait as sent, with jitter, for up to 30 seconds Longer than 30 seconds A backoff beyond one cycle Logs a warning and leaves the image for the next run After a 429, Watchtower also paces later requests to that registry so they cannot empty the bucket again in a burst. Pacing depends on whether the 429 advertised a rate:
429 advertised a rate For 3 minutes after the wait Afterwards Yes One request at a time, at the advertised rate The advertised rate, with bursts up to its budget No One request per retry-after wait, held between 100ms and 30 seconds, or 100ms when the 429 sent none Not paced Retries within a cycle are logged at debug so they do not become notifications. When the retry window is exhausted:
The container is marked Failed for the cycle. One warning naming the container is logged and included in log-based notifications. The report notification lists the container under Failed with the registry error.
data.image-age-determination#Image Age Determ:
When Watchtower detects that a container’s running image differs from the latest available image, it retrieves the image creation timestamp from the registry before deciding whether to update. The process follows the OCI Distribution Spec API:
flowchart TD A[Detect stale image] --> B[Fetch image manifest from registry] B --> C{Multi-platform index?} C -->|Yes| D[Select platform-specific manifest] C -->|No| E[Extract config digest] D --> E E --> F[Fetch config blob from registry] F --> G[Parse JSON — extract 'created' field] G --> H[Calculate image age] classDef step fill:#003343,stroke:#000,stroke-width:2px; classDef decision fill:#003343,stroke:#000,stroke-width:2px; class A,B,D,E,F,G,H step class C decision Manifest fetch: Watchtower sends a GET request to /v2/IMAGE/manifests/TAG with Accept headers covering both OCI and Docker manifest formats. Platform selection: For multi-platform images (manifest lists or OCI indexes), Watchtower selects the manifest matching the runtime OS and architecture. Cross-platform monitoring can be configured via WATCHTOWER_COOLDOWN_PLATFORM_OS and WATCHTOWER_COOLDOWN_PLATFORM_ARCH. For ARM images with multiple variants (e.g., v7, v8), specify WATCHTOWER_COOLDOWN_PLATFORM_VARIANT to disambiguate. Config blob fetch: The manifest’s config digest is used to fetch /v2/IMAGE/blobs/DIGEST. This is a small JSON document (typically <15 KB). Timestamp extraction: The created field from the config JSON is parsed as the image creation time. These requests include the following values:
IMAGE: the image repository, such as library/nginx TAG: the image tag DIGEST: the config digest from the manifest No image layers are downloaded during this process.
Supported registries:
Docker Hub (docker.io) GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io) LinuxServer (lscr.io — internally mapped to ghcr.io) Private registries implementing the OCI Distribution Spec Registries that do not fully implement the OCI Distribution Spec may fail to return image metadata, causing the cooldown check to fail and deferring updates.
data.limitations#Limitations:
The cooldown feature relies on the created field from the image config blob. Several factors can affect the accuracy or availability of this data:
Build timestamp, not push timestamp: The created field records when the image was built, not when it was pushed to the registry. An image built days ago but only just tagged and pushed will appear old, potentially bypassing the intended cooldown window. Manipulated timestamps: A compromised image could include a fabricated creation timestamp, making a freshly published malicious image appear mature. Cooldown is a defense-in-depth measure, not a guarantee of image integrity. Clock skew: If the Watchtower host and the registry have significantly different system clocks, age calculations may be inaccurate. NTP synchronization on all involved hosts is recommended to minimize this risk. When the image creation time is in the future (negative age), Watchtower logs a warning and treats the image as new, deferring the update until the cooldown duration has passed after the creation time. Missing created field: Some registries or image build tools may not populate the created field. When the field is absent, Watchtower cannot determine the image age and defers the update as a safety measure (see the warning above).
data.monitor-only-containers#Monitor-Only Con: Cooldown is not evaluated for containers running in monitor-only mode. Since monitor-only containers are never updated, the cooldown check is skipped to avoid unnecessary registry API calls.
data.multi-platform-images#Multi-Platform Ima:
The cooldown check consumes two pulls per stale container:
One GET for the image index manifest One GET for the platform-specific manifest The subsequent config blob fetch does not count.
data.notifications#Notifications:
Watchtower reports the cooldown status in its notifications. The output varies depending on the outcome:
Image age exceeds cooldownImage within cooldownImage age unavailable nickfedor/watchtower:latest created more than 24 hours ago - eligible for update nickfedor/watchtower:latest created less than 24 hours ago - eligible in 18 hours, 23 minutes nickfedor/watchtower:latest creation time unavailable (cooldown: 24 hours) - deferring update for safety
data.overview#Overview:
When a cooldown is configured, Watchtower checks the creation timestamp of a new image before proceeding with a container update. If the image was published more recently than the configured cooldown period, the update is deferred until the image matures.
This check itself is lightweight, as Watchtower fetches only the image manifest and a small config blob from the registry (typically under 15 KB combined), without downloading any image layers. This also helps to avoid downloading a potentially malicious image.
When Watchtower cannot determine the image creation time, the update is always deferred.
This is a deliberate security decision. It is safer to miss an update than to pull an unverified image. A compromised image published moments ago would not yet have a reliable age signal, and treating the absence of data as “safe to update” would defeat the purpose of the cooldown feature.
The cooldown delay applies to all updates, including security patches.
A critical CVE fix published less than the cooldown duration ago will not be applied until the cooldown expires. Balance your cooldown duration against your risk tolerance and patch SLAs.
data.per-container-label#Per-Container Label:
Individual containers can override the global cooldown using the com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.cooldown-delay label. When set, the label value takes precedence over the global configuration.
Docker ComposeDocker CLIDockerfile services: nginx: image: nginx labels: com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.cooldown-delay: "48h" # ... docker run -d \ --label=com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.cooldown-delay="48h" \ nginx LABEL com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.cooldown-delay="48h" Setting the label to "0" disables cooldown for that container, even when a global cooldown is configured.
LABEL com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.cooldown-delay="0" If a container’s cooldown label cannot be parsed as a valid duration, Watchtower falls back to the global cooldown value. It logs a warning the first time it reads the label for that container, and logs later reads at debug level. No-Pull Precedence
When the no-pull configuration option is enabled globally (or the com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.no-pull label is set on a container), Watchtower does not fetch new images from the registry. Because no new images are pulled, the cooldown check is skipped entirely. This takes precedence over any cooldown configuration — including per-container labels. If you rely on cooldown as a supply-chain defense, ensure that no-pull mode is not inadvertently enabled.
data.per-registry-impact-summary#Per-Registry: Registry Pull Limit Cooldown Impact Docker Hub (unauthenticated) 100 / 6 hours Moderate — may exceed limit with many containers on short intervals Docker Hub (authenticated free) 200 / 6 hours Low — sufficient for most deployments Docker Hub (paid) Unlimited None GHCR.io ~44,000 / minute fill rate (small burst, org-scoped) Low — checks back off for up to 3 minutes when the org bucket is empty. Authenticate to ghcr.io for parallel checks and schedule away from the top of the hour.
data.practical-impact#Practical Impact: Users running Watchtower against Docker Hub with many monitored containers or short polling intervals should be aware that each stale image detected during a cooldown window consumes one or two pulls. Authenticating with a Docker Hub account raises the limit from 100 to 200 pulls, and paid tiers have unlimited pulls.
data.reaching-the-pull-limit#Reaching the Pul:
Over the limit, Docker Hub responds with a 429 whose message reads “You have reached your pull rate limit” and gives no time to wait. The limit holds for the rest of its six-hour window, so Watchtower does not retry within the cycle:
The container is marked Failed for the cycle. One warning naming the container is logged and included in log-based notifications. The next scheduled run checks the container again. Docker Hub’s abuse rate limit returns a plain 429 Too Many Requests instead, which Watchtower handles as described in Handling a 429 Response.
data.registry-usage-impact#Registry Usage Imp:
The cooldown check issues GET requests to the registry for the image manifest and config blob. These requests may count against container registry pull rate limits, which is most relevant for Docker Hub users.
The cooldown check runs only when a newer image is detected (i.e., the container is stale). It does not run on every Watchtower cycle.
data.rolling-restarts#Rolling Restarts: Cooldown is evaluated per-container independently. In rolling restart scenarios, each container’s image age is checked separately. This means containers may update at different times even when using the same image, depending on when each container’s cooldown window expires.
data.scheduling-around-the-hour#Scheduling Ar:
Schedule Watchtower away from the top of the hour:
--schedule "0 17 3 * * *" Interval runs follow the start time, so start Watchtower a few minutes past the hour when polling with --interval.
data.single-platform-images#Single-Platform I:
The cooldown check consumes one pull per stale container:
One GET for the image manifest The subsequent config blob fetch does not count.
data.update-decision#Update Decision:
After determining the image age, Watchtower evaluates four outcomes:
Outcome Condition Behavior Proceeding Image age > cooldown duration The update proceeds normally Deferring Image age ≤ cooldown duration The update is skipped and the container remains on its current image Deferring Image creation time is in the future The update is skipped with a warning until the cooldown duration after the creation time Deferring Image age unavailable The update is skipped for safety flowchart TD A[Stale image detected] --> B{Cooldown configured?} B -->|No| F[Proceed with update] B -->|Yes| C[Fetch image creation time] C --> D{Image age available?} D -->|No| E[Defer update for safety] D -->|Yes| G{Age strictly exceeds cooldown?} G -->|Yes| F G -->|No| H[Defer update — within cooldown] classDef step fill:#003343,stroke:#000,stroke-width:2px; classDef decision fill:#003343,stroke:#000,stroke-width:2px; classDef defer fill:#8B0000,stroke:#000,stroke-width:2px; class A,C,F step class B,D,G decision class E,H defer

data: Watchtower’s lifecycle hooks are a feature that allows monitored containers to execute custom commands at specific points during the container update process. These hooks leverage Docker’s exec API to run commands inside containers.
data.complete-update-cycle#Complete Update Cy:
flowchart TD START([START]) START --> PRECHECK PRECHECK[Pre-check hook] PRECHECK --> SCAN SCAN[Scan for updates
Check images
Find stale containers] SCAN --> DECISION{Stale containers
found?} DECISION -->|No| POSTCHECK DECISION -->|Yes| LOOPSTART LOOPSTART[For each stale container] LOOPSTART --> PREUPDATE PREUPDATE[Pre-update hook] PREUPDATE --> STOP[Stop old container] STOP --> STARTNEW[Start new container] STARTNEW --> POSTUPDATE[Post-update hook] POSTUPDATE --> LOOPEND{All containers
processed?} LOOPEND -->|No| LOOPSTART LOOPEND -->|Yes| POSTCHECK POSTCHECK[Post-check hook] POSTCHECK --> END([END]) classDef hook fill:#406170,stroke:#000,stroke-width:2px; classDef action fill:#003343,stroke:#000,stroke-width:2px; classDef decision fill:#003343,stroke:#000,stroke-width:2px; class PRECHECK,PREUPDATE,POSTUPDATE,POSTCHECK hook class SCAN,STOP,STARTNEW,LOOPSTART action class DECISION,LOOPEND decision
data.custom-timeouts#Custom Timeouts:
By default, hook commands timeout after 1 minute. Override this with timeout labels:
Pre-check timeoutPost-check timeoutPre-update timeoutPost-update timeout LABEL com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.lifecycle.pre-check-timeout="5" LABEL com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.lifecycle.pre-check-timeout="0" LABEL com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.lifecycle.post-check-timeout="5" LABEL com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.lifecycle.post-check-timeout="0" LABEL com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.lifecycle.pre-update-timeout="5" LABEL com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.lifecycle.pre-update-timeout="0" LABEL com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.lifecycle.post-update-timeout="5" LABEL com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.lifecycle.post-update-timeout="0" A timeout must be a whole number of minutes of 0 or more. Any other value, such as -1 or 1.5, logs a warning and uses the 1 minute default.
data.custom-user-execution#Custom User Execut:
By default, hooks run as the monitored container’s configured user and group (uid:gid).
Both global and individual, container-specific uid/gid configurations are supported.
Container labels take precedence over global flags/variables. A UID or GID label outside 0 to 2147483647 logs a warning. The hook then uses the global UID or GID. Without one, it runs as the container’s configured user. Global ConfigurationIndividual Container Configuration Command Line FlagsEnvironment Variables --lifecycle-uid 1000 --lifecycle-gid 1000 WATCHTOWER_LIFECYCLE_UID=1000 WATCHTOWER_LIFECYCLE_GID=1000 LABEL com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.lifecycle.uid="1000" LABEL com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.lifecycle.uid="1000" LABEL com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.lifecycle.gid="1000"
data.debugging#Debugging:
Enable debug logging to see hook execution details:
watchtower --debug --enable-lifecycle-hooks Look for log messages containing:
“Executing pre-check command” “Executing pre-update command” “Executed command” “Command execution failed”
data.defining-hook-commands#Defining Hook Com:
Hook commands are defined using Docker labels on the containers being monitored by Watchtower:
These commands require all necessary tooling (i.e. sh, jq, etc.) to be installed in the monitored container. LABEL com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.lifecycle.pre-check="echo 'Starting update cycle'" LABEL com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.lifecycle.pre-update="echo 'Preparing container for update'" LABEL com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.lifecycle.post-update="echo 'Container updated successfully'" LABEL com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.lifecycle.post-check="echo 'Update cycle completed'" If the container is not running, lifecycle hooks (including pre-update hooks) cannot run, as the stop phase is skipped, and the update proceeds directly to removal (if applicable) or completion.
data.docker-api-integration#Docker API Integr:
Lifecycle hooks utilize Docker’s exec API through the following sequence:
Exec Creation: ExecCreate creates an exec instance with the specified command Exec Start and Output Capture: ExecAttach starts the command and reads its stdout and stderr output to the end Status Monitoring: ExecInspect monitors execution status and exit codes
data.enabling-lifecycle-hooks#Enabling Lifecy:
Lifecycle hooks are disabled by default. Enable them by using the following on the Watchtower container:
Command Line FlagEnvironment Variable --enable-lifecycle-hooks WATCHTOWER_LIFECYCLE_HOOKS=true
data.environment-variables#Environment Variab:
Lifecycle hook commands receive container metadata via the WT_CONTAINER environment variable containing a JSON object with the following fields:
Field Type Description Example name string Container name (may include leading /) "/my-app" or "my-app" id string Full container ID "abc123def456..." image_name string Container image name with tag "nginx:latest" stop_signal string Container’s configured stop signal "SIGTERM" labels object Watchtower-specific labels only {"com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.lifecycle.pre-update": "backup.sh"} The labels object contains only Watchtower-specific labels (those starting with com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.) to keep the JSON payload small and focused on Watchtower configuration.
data.exit-code-confusion#Exit Code Confusion: Exit code 0: Success, continue Exit code 75: Skip this container update Other codes: Fail the entire update process
data.exit-code-handling#Exit Code Handling:
Hook execution results are evaluated based on exit codes, with different behaviors per hook type:
Pre-checkPre-updatePost-updatePost-check Failures are logged but ignored; update process continues Exit Code Description Action 0 Success Continue with update process 75 (EX_TEMPFAIL) Temporary failure Skip updating this container Other Exit Codes Command failure Abort the update process Failures are logged but ignored; update process continues Failures are logged but ignored; update process continues
data.hook-commands-not-executing#Hook Command: Verify --enable-lifecycle-hooks / WATCHTOWER_LIFECYCLE_HOOKS=true is set Check that labels are correctly formatted Ensure container is running (for pre-update hooks)
data.hook-execution-conditions#Hook Execution: Hook Type Scope Timing Conditions Container State Pre-check Per filtered container Beginning of update cycle Command defined + hooks enabled Ignored Pre-update Individual containers being updated Immediately before stopping Command defined + hooks enabled + container running + not restarting Must be running and not restarting Post-update Individual containers successfully updated Immediately after starting new container Command defined + hooks enabled + update successful New container running Post-check Per filtered container End of update cycle Command defined + hooks enabled Ignored
data.hook-output-and-security#Hook Output and:
A hook runs inside the container. Its output therefore comes from whatever runs there, which may be a compromised application or a third-party image. Watchtower treats the output as untrusted text:
It reads the whole output. A command that prints a lot never blocks. It keeps only the last 2 KiB. A leading … marks output whose beginning was dropped. Before the text is logged or sent, it removes: Terminal escape sequences, such as colours, cursor movement, window titles, clipboard writes and hyperlinks Control characters other than newlines, tabs and carriage returns Invisible Unicode format characters, such as bidirectional text controls, zero-width characters and tag characters A carriage return directly before a newline is dropped. Any other carriage return becomes a newline, as do the Unicode line and paragraph separators. It replaces the user information of URLs, such as the dana:s3cret in https://dana:s3cret@git.example.com, with xxxxx. Query values such as ?token=… stay as printed. It puts the output on one line, joining its lines with |. No line of hook output can then pass for one of Watchtower’s own notification lines. The output never changes what Watchtower does. Only the exit code decides whether the update continues, is skipped or fails. Notifications clean all other text from outside Watchtower the same way. They also show at most 1,024 characters of any such text, including hook output. Text from outside Watchtower describes both.
The kept output goes to these places:
Hook When the command succeeds When the command fails Pre-update The debug log, in the “Executed command” line The error-level “Could not update container” log line and the notifications that carry it. The failed container’s error in report templates such as default, json.v1 and the porcelain formats. Pre-check, post-check The debug log, in the “Executed command” line The debug log only Post-update The debug log, in the “Executed command” line The debug log only The HTTP API and its event stream do not include hook output.
Keep secrets out of hook output Notification services are third parties. Debug logs are often shipped to other systems. Apart from the user information of URLs, Watchtower sends hook output as the command printed it. It does not try to recognize other secrets. The replacement runs on the kept 2 KiB. When the cut falls inside a URL, a fragment such as token@host can remain. Guessing from names and formats would hide ordinary output and still miss real secrets.
A failing pre-update hook that prints credentials, for example through set -x, env or curl -v, can send them to every notification service. Write verbose output to a file inside the container or to /dev/null. Print only a short reason when the command fails.
Markup, mentions and look-alike characters Watchtower does not escape the text for each notification service. A service may act on markup or mentions in it:
Discord renders Markdown in a message. It pings only the mentions that the URL’s mentions key lists. Discord counts @everyone and @here as one kind of mention, so listing either one lets both ping. A Discord URL with the /raw path sends the template’s JSON payload as written and ignores the mentions key. Without allowed_mentions in that payload, Discord pings every mention in its content. Email sent with Shoutrrr’s usehtml option renders the text as HTML. Telegram’s HTML and Markdown parse modes format it. Characters that look alike, such as a Cyrillic а in place of a Latin a, stay as written, since removing them would break text in other languages.
data.hook-types#Hook Types:
Watchtower supports four distinct lifecycle hook types that execute at different stages of the update process:
Hook Type Description Execution Timing Pre-check Executed for each filtered container before the update cycle begins Per container, before scanning containers Pre-update Executed before stopping the old container Per container, immediately before stopping Post-update Executed after starting the new container Per container, immediately after starting Post-check Executed for each filtered container after the update cycle completes Per container, after all updates An update cycle that ends before it checks any container runs no check hooks. This happens when the monitored containers cannot be ordered by their dependencies, for example when two of them share a name.
data.overview#Overview:
Lifecycle hooks enable containers to perform custom actions such as:
Graceful shutdown procedures Database backups or migrations Configuration validation Notification systems Cleanup operations
data.permission-issues#Permission Issues: Use appropriate UID/GID labels Ensure user has permissions to execute commands Check container’s user configuration

data.synology-dsm-graceful-shutdown#Synology:
This is an example implementation that requires additional testing and validation. There is a well-known issue with Synology devices sending warning notifications when containers are stopped by anything other than the Synology’s Docker service. This can be problematic when using tools like Watchtower that stop and restart containers.
The examples/lifecycle-hooks/synology-stop directory provides examples for implementing graceful shutdowns using Synology’s DSM Web API. This includes both shell script and Go implementations that authenticate with DSM, stop containers gracefully, and handle session management.
See the synology-stop README for detailed setup instructions, environment variables, and deployment examples using docker-compose.
