data.automatic-detection#Automatic Detection:
In most cases, no additional configuration is required. Watchtower automatically detects dependencies from:
Docker Compose depends_on declarations Existing Docker links network_mode: service:SERVICE and network_mode: container:CONTAINER configurations volumes_from configurations Docker Compose Considerations
When using Docker Compose, Watchtower leverages depends_on declarations for dependency detection. Dependencies are resolved using service names, not container names. Ensure your depends_on references service names correctly.
Rolling restart is currently not supported when used in combination with linked-containers.
This limitation exists because linked-containers require coordinated updates across dependency chains, which conflicts with the incremental nature of rolling restarts.
data.common-issues#Common Issues: Watchtower reports each of the following dependency problems once per container. The first scan that finds a problem logs and notifies it as a warning. Later scans log it at debug level. Every scan still skips a container that depends on itself or sits in a circular dependency, and lists it as skipped in the session report. A container depends on itself when one of its dependencies names it by its container name or by its own Compose service. A skipped container is not restarted when another of its dependencies is updated. A depends-on entry that names no container is only ignored, and its container is still checked and updated. A recreated container or a restart of Watchtower reports the problem again.
data.complex-dependency-chains#Complex Depend: services: web: image: nginx depends_on: - api api: image: myapi depends_on: - database - cache database: image: postgres cache: image: redis In this scenario, Watchtower will update containers in the order: cache, database, api, web.
data.containers-not-updating-in-expected-orde:
Check:
Verify dependency labels are correctly formatted Ensure container names match exactly Check Docker Compose service names vs container names
data.containers-skipped-due-to-circular-depen: If you see “Skipping container update (circular dependency)” warnings, check your dependency declarations for cycles. Solution: Review and remove circular dependencies. For example, if A depends on B and B depends on A, remove one of the dependencies or restructure your services.
data.debugging-commands#Debugging Commands:
Enable verbose logging to inspect dependency detection:
docker run --rm \ -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \ nickfedor/watchtower \ --debug \ --run-once Check container labels:
docker inspect container_name | jq '.[0].Config.Labels'
data.dependencies-on-unmonitored-containers#D:
A container that Watchtower does not monitor is left alone, including when a monitored container depends on it. Containers are excluded from monitoring by the container selection options, such as the enable label, the disable lists, image filters, and scopes.
A dependency on an unmonitored container is ignored when ordering updates and restarting dependents. A dependency that names an unmonitored container exactly never resolves to a different, monitored container with a similar name. A service name whose service in the container’s own Compose project is unmonitored never resolves to the same service in another project.
data.dependency-detection#Dependency Detectio:
Watchtower detects container dependencies from labels and from each container’s Docker configuration.
Labels are checked in the following priority order, and only the first one present is used:
Watchtower depends-on label (com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.depends-on) Docker Compose depends_on label (com.docker.compose.depends_on) An empty Watchtower depends-on label counts as absent, so the Docker Compose depends_on label is used instead when Compose detection is enabled.
The Docker configuration always counts as well, whichever label is present:
Docker links and network mode (legacy Docker linking, network_mode: service:SERVICE for a Compose service, and network_mode: container:CONTAINER for a container name or ID) Volumes from another container (volumes_from in Compose, --volumes-from in the Docker CLI) A container named by both a label and the Docker configuration is a single dependency.
data.disable-docker-compose-depends-on#Disabl:
If you want to disable automatic dependency detection from the Docker Compose depends_on configuration while preserving other dependency sources, use the following configuration:
Docker ComposeDocker CLI services: watchtower: image: nickfedor/watchtower environment: - WATCHTOWER_USE_COMPOSE_DEPENDS_ON=false docker run -d \ --name watchtower \ -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \ nickfedor/watchtower \ --use-compose-depends-on=false This disables parsing of the com.docker.compose.depends_on label while still honoring:
Watchtower’s explicit com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.depends-on label Legacy Docker links Network mode dependencies (network_mode: service:SERVICE and network_mode: container:CONTAINER) Volumes from another container (volumes_from)
data.docker-compose-depends-on-label#Docker C:
Watchtower automatically recognizes Docker Compose’s depends_on relationships:
services: web: image: nginx depends_on: - database database: image: postgres The com.docker.compose.depends_on label is automatically set by Docker Compose and parsed by Watchtower to extract service names and support implicitly restarting linked services.
Docker Compose depends_on Restart Behavior
Docker Compose’s depends_on has a restart attribute in the long-form syntax:
services: web: depends_on: database: condition: service_healthy restart: true Watchtower does not support using this to control implicit restarts, because this is an explicit, opt-in feature that defaults to false when omitted, such as when using the short-form syntax.
data.docker-links-and-network-mode#Docker Lin:
For legacy Docker links, and for containers that use another container’s network (network_mode: service:SERVICE or network_mode: container:CONTAINER in Compose, --network container:CONTAINER in the Docker CLI), Watchtower treats these as implicit dependencies:
# Container with explicit link docker run --link database:db nginx # Container using another container's network docker run --network container:CONTAINER nginx Replace CONTAINER with the name or ID of the container whose network to use.
These count as dependencies even when a depends-on or Compose depends_on label names other containers, because the container cannot run without the container whose network it uses. The same applies to volumes_from (--volumes-from): the container is always ordered after the container whose volumes it uses.
data.explicit-dependencies#Explicit Dependenc:
For cases where automatic detection is insufficient, use the Watchtower depends-on label:
DockerfileDocker Compose FROM nginx:latest # Declare dependencies on database and cache services LABEL com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.depends-on="postgres,redis" services: web: image: nginx labels: - com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.depends-on=postgres,redis postgres: image: postgres redis: image: redis
data.ignored-depends-on-entries#Ignored Depen: If you see “Ignoring depends-on entry that names no container” warnings, the named com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.depends-on entry matched no container. Solution: Use the exact container name, a Compose service name, or a project-qualified service name such as myproject-db.
data.legacy-docker-links#Legacy Docker Links:
For applications using traditional Docker linking:
Docker Run CommandsWatchtower Behavior # Start database docker run -d --name mysql mysql:8.0 # Start web app with link docker run -d --name webapp --link mysql:db nginx Watchtower automatically detects the link and ensures webapp is stopped before mysql updates, and mysql restarts before webapp.
data.microservices-architecture#Microservices:
For complex applications with multiple services:
Docker ComposeDependency Graph services: api-gateway: image: nginx depends_on: - auth-service - user-service auth-service: image: auth-service depends_on: - redis user-service: image: user-service depends_on: - postgres redis: image: redis postgres: image: postgres postgres → user-service redis → auth-service auth-service → api-gateway user-service → api-gateway Update order: postgres, redis, user-service, auth-service, api-gateway
data.missing-dependencies#Missing Dependencie:
Symptoms: Containers update out of order or fail to connect after updates.
Debug: Enable debug logging to see detected dependencies:
watchtower --debug Look for log messages like:
“Found container dependencies”, which lists each container’s dependencies once per scan
data.mysql-wordpress-scenario#MySQL-WordPress:
Consider a classic WordPress setup with MySQL database:
Docker ComposeUpdate Process services: wordpress: image: wordpress:latest depends_on: - mysql environment: WORDPRESS_DB_HOST: mysql mysql: image: mysql:8.0 environment: MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: 'DB_ROOT_PASSWORD' Replace DB_ROOT_PASSWORD with a root password for the database, inside the single quotes so that YAML reads every character as part of it. Inside the quotes, write each ' as ''. Write each $ as $$, because Compose reads a $ as the start of a variable even inside quotes.
When Watchtower detects a MySQL update:
Dependency Detection: Identifies that wordpress depends on mysql Stop Order: Stops wordpress first, then mysql Update Order: Updates and restarts mysql first, then wordpress This prevents WordPress from losing database connectivity during the update.
data.network-mode-dependencies#Network Mode D:
Containers using network_mode: service:SERVICE:
Docker ComposeWatchtower Behavior services: sidecar: image: sidecar network_mode: service:main-app main-app: image: main-app The sidecar container is treated as dependent on main-app, ensuring proper update sequencing.
data.overview#Overview:
Watchtower, by default, ensures that interdependent containers are updated in the correct order to maintain application stability. It automatically detects container dependencies through various mechanisms and uses topological sorting to determine the optimal update sequence.
When containers depend-upon each other (such as a web application depending on a database), updating them in the wrong order can cause service disruptions.
Watchtower addresses this by:
Detecting dependencies through Docker links, labels, and network configurations Performing topological sorting to determine the correct update order Stopping containers in reverse dependency order (dependents first - i.e., web app before database) Restarting containers in dependency order (dependencies first - i.e., database before web app) This ensures that dependent services are stopped before their dependencies are updated, and dependencies are available when dependents restart.
data.restarting-dependent-containers#Restarti:
When a container is updated, Watchtower also restarts the containers that depend on it, directly or through other restarted containers, without updating their images. Dependents are found with the same dependency graph that orders the update, so the containers restarted and the update order always agree.
A Watchtower container restarts when a container it depends on restarts, such as a VPN container it shares a network with. A container that names a Watchtower container exactly, by container name or ID, restarts when that Watchtower container is updated. The name without its replica number (such as infra-watchtower for infra-watchtower-1) also works when exactly one Watchtower container has it, so it names nothing when the service runs several replicas. Containers in a circular dependency are neither updated nor restarted.
data.topological-sorting#Topological Sorting:
Watchtower uses topological sorting to determine the correct update order. This algorithm:
Builds a dependency graph from all detected relationships Detects cycles and sets aside every container in one Produces a linear ordering where dependencies precede dependents Containers in a circular dependency are skipped and reported as skipped, while the rest of the update continues. Ensure your dependency graph is acyclic so those containers are updated.
data.update-order#Update Order:
When updates are needed, Watchtower follows this sequence:
Identify all containers requiring updates Expand the set to include all containers in the dependency chain Sort containers using topological order (dependencies first) Stop containers in reverse topological order (dependents first) Update and restart containers in topological order (dependencies first) This ensures that:
Dependent services are stopped before their dependencies change Dependencies are fully restarted before dependents attempt to connect
data.watchtower-depends-on-label#Watchtower D:
The com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.depends-on label allows explicit declaration of dependencies:
LABEL com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.depends-on="database,redis" This label accepts a comma-separated list of container names that must be available before this container starts. This supports referencing containers from other Docker Compose projects or stacks, enabling cross-project dependency management.
An entry may also name a Docker Compose service, such as db or my-database, or a project-qualified service, such as myproject-db. A service name resolves to every replica of that service.
A service name used in more than one Compose project, such as db, resolves to the service in the labeled container’s own project when that project has one. Otherwise it resolves to the service in every project that has it, so the container restarts when any of them is updated. When the service in its own project is unmonitored, the entry is left alone instead (see Dependencies on Unmonitored Containers). Use the container name or a project-qualified service name, such as myproject-db, to depend on only one of them.
An entry that names no container is ignored and logged as a warning.

data:
Watchtower supports private Docker image registries.
In many cases, accessing a private registry requires a valid username and password (i.e., credentials). In order to operate in such an environment, Watchtower needs to know the credentials to access the registry. The credentials can be provided to Watchtower in a configuration file called config.json.
There are two ways to generate this configuration file:
The configuration file can be created manually. Call docker login REGISTRY_NAME and share the resulting configuration file.
data.creating-the-configuration-file-manually:
Create a new configuration file with the following syntax and a base64 encoded username and password auth string:
{ "auths": { "REGISTRY_NAME": { "auth": "BASE64_CREDENTIALS" } } } Replace the following:
REGISTRY_NAME: the name of your private registry, such as registry.example.org BASE64_CREDENTIALS: the base64 encoding of USERNAME:PASSWORD, your user name and password for the registry joined by a colon
data.credential-helpers#Credential helpers:
Some private Docker registries (the most prominent probably being AWS ECR) use non-standard ways of authentication. To be able to use this together with Watchtower, we need to use a credential helper.
To keep the image size small we’ve decided to not include any helpers in the Watchtower image, instead we’ll put the helper in a separate container and mount it using volumes.
data.docker-config-path#Docker Config path:
By default, Watchtower will look for the config.json file in /, but this can be changed by setting the DOCKER_CONFIG environment variable to the directory path where your config is located. This is useful for setups where the config.json file is changed while the Watchtower instance is running, as the changes will not be picked up for a mounted file if the inode changes.
For example:
services: watchtower: image: nickfedor/watchtower environment: DOCKER_CONFIG: /config volumes: - /etc/watchtower/config/:/config/ - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock
data.example#Example:
Here is an example implementation for use with the amazon-ecr-credential-helper :
Use the Dockerfile below to build the amazon-ecr-credential-helper image in a volume that may be mounted onto your Watchtower container.
Create the Dockerfile:
FROM golang:1.25 ENV GO111MODULE off ENV CGO_ENABLED 0 ENV REPO github.com/awslabs/amazon-ecr-credential-helper/ecr-login/cli/docker-credential-ecr-login RUN go get -u $REPO RUN rm /go/bin/docker-credential-ecr-login RUN go build \ -o /go/bin/docker-credential-ecr-login \ /go/src/$REPO WORKDIR /go/bin/ Use the following commands to build the aws-ecr-dock-cred-helper and store it’s output in a volume:
Create a volume to store the command (once built):
docker volume create helper Build the container:
docker build -t aws-ecr-dock-cred-helper . Build the command and store it in the new volume in the /go/bin directory:
docker run -d --rm --name aws-cred-helper \ --volume helper:/go/bin aws-ecr-dock-cred-helper Create a configuration file for Docker, and store it in $HOME/.docker/config.json. Replace AWS_ACCOUNT_ID with your AWS account ID and AWS_ECR_REGION with the AWS Region of your Amazon ECR registry:
{ "credsStore" : "ecr-login", "HttpHeaders" : { "User-Agent" : "Docker-Client/19.03.1 (linux)" }, "auths" : { "AWS_ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.AWS_ECR_REGION.amazonaws.com" : {} }, "credHelpers": { "AWS_ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.AWS_ECR_REGION.amazonaws.com" : "ecr-login" } } services: # Check for new images and restart things if a new image exists # for any of our containers. watchtower: image: nickfedor/watchtower:latest volumes: - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock - .docker/config.json:/config.json - helper:/go/bin environment: - HOME=/ - PATH=$PATH:/go/bin - AWS_REGION=us-west-1 volumes: helper: external: true A few additional notes:
The volume (helper, in this case) MUST be set to external: true, otherwise Docker Compose will preface it with the directory name.
Note that “credsStore” : “ecr-login” is needed - and in theory if you have that you can remove the credHelpers section
This may be able to run in an EC2 instance that has credentials assigned to it, so no keys are needed; however, you may need to include the AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY environment variables as well.
Then, mount the ~/.aws directory to / in the container.
data.sharing-the-docker-configuration-file#Sh:
To pull an image from a private registry, docker login needs to be called first, to get access to the registry. The provided credentials are stored in a configuration file called .docker/config.json in your home directory. This configuration file can be directly used by Watchtower. In this case, the creation of an additional configuration file is not necessary.
When the Docker container is started, pass the configuration file to Watchtower:
docker run [...] -v "HOME_DIR/.docker/config.json:/config.json" nickfedor/watchtower Replace HOME_DIR with the absolute path of your home directory, such as /home/dana.
When creating the Watchtower container via Docker Compose, use the following lines:
services: watchtower: image: nickfedor/watchtower:latest volumes: - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock - HOME_DIR/.docker/config.json:/config.json # ... Replace HOME_DIR with the absolute path of your home directory, such as /home/dana.
data.using-a-private-registry-on-a-local-host:
To use a private registry hosted locally, make sure to correctly specify the registry host in both config.json and the docker run command or docker-compose file. Valid hosts are localhost[:PORT], HOST:PORT, or any multi-part domain.name or IP-address with or without a port.
Examples:
localhost -> localhost/myimage 127.0.0.1 -> 127.0.0.1/myimage:mytag registry.example.com -> registry.example.com/myorganization/myimage other-lan-host:80 -> other-lan-host:80/imagename:latest The required auth string can be generated as follows:
echo -n 'USERNAME:PASSWORD' | base64 Replace USERNAME and PASSWORD with your user name and password for the registry.
Username and Password for GCloud
For gcloud, we’ll use _json_key as our username and the content of gcloudauth.json as the password.
bash echo -n "_json_key:$(cat gcloudauth.json)" | base64 -w0 When the Watchtower Docker container is started, the created configuration file needs to be passed to the container:
docker run [...] -v "CONFIG_DIR/config.json:/config.json" nickfedor/watchtower Replace CONFIG_DIR with the absolute path of the directory that holds the configuration file. Docker reads a relative path as the name of a volume.
data.using-private-docker-hub-images#Using Pr:
To access private repositories on Docker Hub, REGISTRY_NAME should be https://index.docker.io/v1/. The registry domain does not have to be specified in docker run or docker-compose.
Like Docker, Watchtower will use the Docker Hub registry and its credentials when no registry domain is specified. Watchtower will recognize credentials with REGISTRY_NAME set to index.docker.io, but the Docker CLI will not.

data: Registry mirrors provide alternative locations for pulling Docker images, useful when access to the default registry is slow, unreliable, or restricted by network policy. Watchtower uses these mirrors when checking whether containers need updates, ensuring it can detect new images even when the primary registry is unreachable.
data.authentication-issues#Authentication Iss: If a mirror requires authentication, configure credentials in the Docker daemon (e.g., docker login). Watchtower uses the same credentials for mirrors as for the canonical registry.
data.command-line-configuration#Command-Line:
Mirrors can also be set via the dockerd command line:
dockerd --registry-mirror https://mirror.example.com
data.configuration-file#Configuration File:
Linux: /etc/docker/daemon.json Windows: C:\ProgramData\docker\config\daemon.json Rootless mode: ~/.config/docker/daemon.json After making changes, restart the daemon:
sudo systemctl restart docker
data.configuration-format#Configuration Forma:
Docker’s registry-mirrors setting is a Docker Hub mirror list. Add Hub mirrors under the registry-mirrors key:
{ "registry-mirrors": [ "https://mirror.example.com" ] } When multiple mirrors are listed, they are tried in order until one succeeds.
data.configuring-registry-mirrors#Configuring: Registry mirrors are configured in the Docker daemon, not in Watchtower itself.
data.corporate-proxy-environment#Corporate Pr:
When using internal mirrors that may use self-signed certificates:
{ "registry-mirrors": [ "https://harbor.example.com" ], "insecure-registries": [ "harbor.example.com" ] }
data.how-watchtower-uses-mirrors#How Watchtow:
When checking if a Docker Hub image has been updated, Watchtower resolves the mirror to use in this order:
Configured mirrors — The daemon mirror list is tried first. Canonical registry — If all mirrors fail without a rate-limit (429) response, Watchtower falls back to index.docker.io. A 429 stops the check instead of trying Docker Hub. The first mirror to successfully respond with the image manifest wins. This means a fast, nearby mirror is preferred over Docker Hub.
Images on other registries, such as ghcr.io and lscr.io, skip the mirror list and use their own host.
data.mirrors-not-being-used#Mirrors Not Being:
Verify daemon configuration — Confirm that /etc/docker/daemon.json contains valid JSON and the Docker daemon has been restarted since the last change.
Enable debug logging — Run Watchtower with debug logging to see mirror resolution in action:
docker run -d --name watchtower \ -e WATCHTOWER_DEBUG=true \ -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \ nickfedor/watchtower Look for log output containing Resolved registry mirror configuration. A non-Hub image logs Skipping Docker Hub registry mirrors for non-Hub image and is not a misconfiguration.
Check network access — Ensure the host can reach the mirror URLs (e.g., curl -I https://mirror.example.com/v2/).
Verify mirror content — Confirm the mirror is operational and has the required images.
data.multiple-mirrors-with-redundancy#Multipl:
Mirrors are tried in the order listed. If the first is unreachable, the next is used:
{ "registry-mirrors": [ "https://primary-mirror.example.com", "https://backup-mirror.example.com" ] }
data.overview#Overview:
When the Docker daemon is configured with registry mirrors, Watchtower automatically detects and uses them during its update checks. This means:
Digest comparisons — For Docker Hub images, Watchtower fetches manifests from mirrors before falling back to the canonical registry, so it can detect updates even when Docker Hub is inaccessible. Docker Hub only — Daemon registry-mirrors apply to Docker Hub (docker.io, index.docker.io, and bare image names). GHCR, lscr.io, and other registries are checked on their canonical host. Mirror support in Watchtower covers digest comparison only — determining whether a newer image exists. The actual image pull is handled by the Docker daemon, which already uses configured mirrors natively.
data.related-features#Related Features: Private Registries — Authenticating with private image registries Secure Connections — TLS and certificate configuration
data.single-global-mirror#Single Global Mirro:
A single mirror used for Docker Hub:
{ "registry-mirrors": [ "https://docker-mirror.example.com" ] }
data.ssltls-errors#SSL/TLS Errors:
For mirrors using self-signed or internal CA certificates, add them to the insecure-registries list:
{ "insecure-registries": ["internal-mirror.example.com"] } Insecure registries accept HTTPS with untrusted certificates. Only use this for internal mirrors under your control.

data:
By default, Watchtower is set-up to monitor the local Docker daemon (the same daemon running the Watchtower container itself). However, it is possible to configure Watchtower to monitor a remote Docker endpoint. When starting the Watchtower container you can specify a remote Docker endpoint with either the --host flag or the DOCKER_HOST environment variable:
docker run -d \ --name watchtower \ nickfedor/watchtower --host "tcp://192.0.2.10:2375" or
docker run -d \ --name watchtower \ -e DOCKER_HOST="tcp://192.0.2.10:2375" \ nickfedor/watchtower Replace 192.0.2.10 with the address of your remote Docker host.
Note in both of the examples above that it is unnecessary to mount the /var/run/docker.sock into the Watchtower container.

By default, Watchtower stops and removes the other Watchtower instances it finds on its Docker host, so only one instance runs. To run several instances on one host, give each one its own scope. Each instance then:
Manages only the containers in its scope Removes only the other instances in its scope Two instances can’t share a scope. When an instance starts, it removes the other instances in its scope.
data.defining-a-scope#Defining a Scope:
An instance takes its scope from one of these:
Its scope configuration option The com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.scope label of its own container, when that option is not set The second source is described in Scope From the Container Label.
The instance then manages each container whose com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.scope label names that scope, including its own Watchtower container.
Without the scope label on its own container, a scoped instance counts as unscoped to other instances. An unscoped instance on the same host then removes it at startup.
data.example-one-scope#Example: One Scope:
In this Docker Compose file, watchtower manages app and itself:
services: app: image: myapps/app labels: - "com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.scope=myscope" watchtower: image: nickfedor/watchtower volumes: - "/var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock" environment: - WATCHTOWER_SCOPE=myscope labels: - "com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.scope=myscope"
data.example-scope-from-a-label#Example: Scop:
In this Docker Compose file, watchtower has no scope configuration option and takes the scope myscope from its label:
services: watchtower: image: nickfedor/watchtower volumes: - "/var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock" labels: - "com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.scope=myscope"
data.example-unscoped-instance#Example: Unsco:
In this Docker Compose file, watchtower manages all three apps and itself, and it leaves the myscope containers from the first example alone:
services: app-a: image: myapps/app-a app-b: image: myapps/app-b labels: - "com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.scope=none" app-c: image: myapps/app-c labels: - "com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.scope=" watchtower: image: nickfedor/watchtower volumes: - "/var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock" environment: - WATCHTOWER_SCOPE=none
data.scope-from-the-container-label#Scope Fro: Without the scope configuration option, Watchtower reads its scope from the com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.scope label of its own container. An instance can therefore be scoped by that label alone.
data.unscoped-containers#Unscoped Containers:
A container has no scope when its com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.scope label is:
Missing Empty Set to none
data.unscoped-instances#Unscoped Instances:
An instance has no scope when either of these is true:
Its scope configuration option is set to none. Neither its scope configuration option nor its own label sets a scope. An unscoped instance:
Manages only unscoped containers Removes only other unscoped instances Unscoped and scoped instances can run on the same host, since each leaves the other’s containers alone.
data.when-the-label-cannot-be-read#When the L:
If Watchtower cannot inspect its own container at startup, then it exits with an error rather than run without a scope.
Before it exits, it disables its container’s restart policy. Start it again once the cause is fixed. If the restart policy cannot be disabled, then Watchtower reports that as an error too. The restart policy may then start Watchtower again. Setting the scope configuration option avoids the dependency on the label. The option takes precedence over the label, and none counts as a set value.

data.basic-tutorial#Basic Tutorial:
This is not a comprehensive guide and is merely a simple tutorial to illustrate a basic test deployment.
The following tutorial is intended to provide a basic walkthrough for manually setting up Watchtower to perform container updates on a Docker host that has enabled access to the Docker daemon using TLS.
This largely follow’s Docker’s guide for setting up TLS on the Docker host.
Configuring Docker to accept network connections has critical security implications that can leave you vulnerable to unauthorized access. You are highly encouraged to perform your own due diligence to mitigate these risks.
data.certificate-generation#Certificate Gener: Generate self-signed certificates for testing (replace with proper certificates for production):
data.certificate-management#Certificate Manag:
This documentation is not intended to be a guide on TLS/mTLS certificate deployment or management. Manual certificate management might be acceptable for smaller deployments; however, there are solutions for automating certificate management. If you are exposing your Docker daemon to external network connections, then both proper TLS setup and management is a highly recommended.
Here are just a few available solutions:
Step-CA : Smallstep’s private, self-hostable certificate authority. [Tutorial ] Vault : HashiCorp’s secret management tool with PKI secrets engine for certificate generation CFSSL : Cloudflare’s PKI toolkit for certificate management
data.create-a-ca-key-and-certificate#Create a:
Generate a 4096-bit RSA private key for the Certificate Authority and save it to ca-key.pem:
openssl genrsa -aes256 -out ca-key.pem 4096 Make sure to take note of the passphrase Create a self-signed X.509 certificate for the Certificate Authority (valid for 365 days) using the private key and save it to ca.pem:
openssl req -new -x509 -days 365 -key ca-key.pem -sha256 -out ca.pem -subj "/C=US/ST=State/L=City/O=Org/CN=ca"
data.create-a-client-key-and-certificate#Crea:
Generate a 4096-bit RSA private key for the client certificate and save it to key.pem:
openssl genrsa -out key.pem 4096 Generate a certificate signing request (CSR) for the client with common name “client” and save it to client.csr:
openssl req -subj '/CN=client' -new -key key.pem -out client.csr Sign the client CSR with the CA certificate, creating a client certificate valid for 365 days with the client authentication extension, and save it to cert.pem:
echo "extendedKeyUsage = clientAuth" > extfile-client.cnf This makes the key suitable for client authentication. openssl x509 -req -days 365 -sha256 -in client.csr -CA ca.pem -CAkey ca-key.pem -CAcreateserial -out cert.pem -extfile extfile-client.cnf
data.create-a-server-key-and-certificate#Crea:
Generate a 4096-bit RSA private key for the server certificate and save it to server-key.pem:
openssl genrsa -out server-key.pem 4096 Generate a certificate signing request (CSR) for the server with common name “localhost” and save it to server.csr:
openssl req -subj "/CN=$HOST" -sha256 -new -key server-key.pem -out server.csr Sign the server CSR with the CA certificate, creating a server certificate valid for 365 days with the specified extensions, and save it to server-cert.pem:
echo "subjectAltName = DNS:$HOST,IP:192.0.2.20,IP:127.0.0.1" > extfile-server.cnf IP:192.0.2.20 is an example IP. Replace it with your host’s actual IP. $HOST typically resolves to the hostname. Change this as necessary (i.e. localhost for testing) echo "extendedKeyUsage = serverAuth" >> extfile-server.cnf This sets the Docker daemon key’s extended usage attributes to be used only for server authentication. openssl x509 -req -days 365 -sha256 -in server.csr -CA ca.pem -CAkey ca-key.pem -CAcreateserial -out server-cert.pem -extfile extfile-server.cnf
data.docker-api-version#Docker API Version: Argument: --api-version Environment Variable: DOCKER_API_VERSION Type: String Default: Auto-negotiated This provides the ability to manually specify the Docker API version. The default version autonegotiation should be sufficient for normal use cases.
data.docker-host-url#Docker Host URL: Argument: --host Environment Variable: DOCKER_HOST Type: String Default: unix:///var/run/docker.sock Specifying multiple connections, such as both the local socket (i.e. /var/run/docker.sock) and a remote host is not supported. This is required for connections to any Docker host. The use of tcp:// or https:// schemes is required when using a TLS connection. An https:// host is treated as tcp://.
data.docker-socket-proxies#Docker Socket Prox:
You are highly encouraged to perform your own due diligence before using any software that interacts directly with the Docker socket. Docker socket proxies provide a security layer between applications and the Docker daemon by filtering API calls and preventing unrestricted access to the Docker socket.
While this documentation focuses on TLS-based connections, socket proxies represent another approach for securing Docker daemon access in environments where full socket exposure is undesirable.
Refer to the documentation for the Docker Host URL to connect Watchtower to a Docker socket proxy.
The following projects are examples of Docker socket proxies:
https://github.com/Tecnativa/docker-socket-proxy https://github.com/11notes/docker-socket-proxy https://github.com/linuxserver/docker-socket-proxy https://github.com/wollomatic/socket-proxy
data.examples#Examples:
Replace the following:
CERT_DIR: the absolute path of a directory that holds only the client’s ca.pem, cert.pem and key.pem files HOST: the host name or IP address of the Docker host, as named in its server certificate. Enclose an IPv6 address in brackets, such as [2001:db8::1]. Docker CLIDocker Compose docker run -d \ --name watchtower \ -v "CERT_DIR:/etc/ssl/docker:ro" \ nickfedor/watchtower --host tcp://HOST:2376 --cert-path /etc/ssl/docker --tlsverify Parameter Description --name watchtower Assigns the name “watchtower” to the container for easy identification and management. -v "CERT_DIR:/etc/ssl/docker:ro" Mounts the local certificate directory to the container’s SSL directory as read-only. nickfedor/watchtower Specifies the Docker image to run, which is the Watchtower container image. --host tcp://HOST:2376 Sets the Docker host to connect to via TCP on port 2376. --cert-path /etc/ssl/docker Defines the path inside the container where TLS certificates are located. --tlsverify Enables TLS verification for secure connections to the Docker host. If using -e flags to pass environment variables, then remember to place them before the nickfedor/watchtower image reference. services: watchtower: image: nickfedor/watchtower environment: - DOCKER_HOST=tcp://HOST:2376 - DOCKER_CERT_PATH=/etc/ssl/docker - DOCKER_TLS_VERIFY=1 volumes: - CERT_DIR:/etc/ssl/docker:ro restart: unless-stopped Parameter Description image: nickfedor/watchtower Specifies the Docker image for the Watchtower service. - DOCKER_HOST=tcp://HOST:2376 Sets the Docker host connection URL. - DOCKER_CERT_PATH=/etc/ssl/docker Specifies the path to the directory containing TLS certificates. - DOCKER_TLS_VERIFY=1 Enables TLS verification for secure connections. CERT_DIR:/etc/ssl/docker:ro Mounts the local certificate directory to the container’s SSL directory as read-only. restart: unless-stopped Configures the container to restart automatically unless it was manually stopped.
data.insecure-scheme-with-tls-verification#In:
When TLS verification is enabled and the Docker host URL uses http://, Watchtower logs the following warning:
TLS verification is enabled but DOCKER_HOST uses insecure scheme ‘http://’. Consider using ’tcp://’ or disable TLS verification. Possible Solutions:
If using a secure connection, then use tcp://. If using http://, then disable TLS verification.
data.key-and-certificate-management#Key and C:
Remove both the certificate signing requests (client.csr and server.csr) and extensions config files (extfile-server.cnf and extfile-client.cnf) after generating the server (server-cert.pem) and client cert.pem certificates:
rm -v client.csr server.csr extfile-server.cnf extfile-client.cnf Update the file permissions of the ca-key.pem, server-key.pem, and key.pem secret keys:
sudo chmod -v 0400 ca-key.pem server-key.pem key.pem Remove ca.pem, server-cert.pem, and cert.pem file write access:
sudo chmod -v 0444 ca.pem server-cert.pem cert.pem Create the /etc/docker/certs directory if it doesn’t exist:
sudo mkdir -p /etc/docker/certs Copy the server-specific files:
sudo cp ca.pem ca-key.pem server-cert.pem server-key.pem /etc/docker/certs/ (Optional): Copy the client-specific files:
sudo cp cert.pem key.pem /etc/docker/certs/ Ensure root ownership:
sudo chown root:root /etc/docker/certs/* Set directory-level access:
sudo chmod 0755 /etc/docker/certs/ Verify the files:
ls -la /etc/docker/certs/ Output should show files with -r-------- for keys and -r--r--r-- for certs. (Optional) Remove the original files (in the original directory, not /etc/docker/certs):
rm -v {ca,ca-key,server-cert,server-key,cert,key}.pem The server files (ca.pem, server-key.pem, server-cert.pem) stay on the daemon host. The client’s files (ca.pem, key.pem, and cert.pem) can be moved the client’s Docker directory (e.g. ~/.docker/).
data.local-socket-with-tls-verification#Local:
When TLS verification is enabled and the Docker host URL is not configured or uses unix://, Watchtower logs the following warning:
TLS verification is enabled but DOCKER_HOST uses local socket ‘unix://’. TLS is not applicable for local sockets. Consider disabling TLS verification. Possible Solutions:
If the Docker host URL is not configured, then the default unix:///var/run/docker.sock is used. If using a local socket (i.e. unix://), then disable TLS verification.
data.missing-tls-certificates#Missing TLS Cer:
In order for Watchtower’s Docker client to connect to the Docker daemon via TLS, the certificates must be provided to the Watchtower container.
If the certificates are available via the host filesystem of the Watchtower container’s Docker host, then this can be accomplished using bind mounts . Other options, such as building a custom Watchtower image with the certificates, are outside the scope of this documentation.
Refer to the documentation for the TLS Certificate Path and the examples.
data.other-common-mistakes#Other Common Mista: Using tcp:// without --tlsverify: This disables TLS, potentially allowing insecure connections. Mismatched certificate paths: Ensure DOCKER_CERT_PATH points to the correct directory containing cert.pem and key.pem. Expired or invalid certificates: Check certificate validity and SAN fields matching the host. Firewall blocking TLS port: Ensure port 2376 is open for remote connections.
data.overview#Overview:
Watchtower supports secure TLS connections to Docker hosts through its usage of Docker’s Go SDK to create a Docker client.
It is highly recommended to review Docker’s documentation:
https://docs.docker.com/engine/daemon/remote-access/ https://docs.docker.com/engine/security/protect-access https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/dockerd/#daemon-socket-option Docker has retired the Docker Machine project that was previously noted in Watchtower’s documentation.
data.setup-the-docker-daemon-with-tls#Setup t:
This assumes Docker is already installed on the host system. Edit or create /etc/docker/daemon.json to enable TLS and TCP listening:
{ "tls": true, "tlscacert": "/etc/docker/certs/ca.pem", "tlscert": "/etc/docker/certs/server-cert.pem", "tlskey": "/etc/docker/certs/server-key.pem", "hosts": ["unix:///var/run/docker.sock", "tcp://0.0.0.0:2376"] } "tls": true enables TLS verification. "hosts": ["unix:///var/run/docker.sock", "tcp://0.0.0.0:2376"] adds TCP listening on port 2376 and retains the Unix socket for local access. Alternatively, use dockerd flags in /etc/systemd/system/docker.service.d/override.conf for overrides without editing daemon.json. Restart the daemon:
sudo systemctl restart docker Verify the daemon is listening:
sudo netstat -tlnp | grep 2376
data.tls-certificate-path#TLS Certificate Pat: Argument: --cert-path Environment Variable: DOCKER_CERT_PATH Type: String Default: None This specifies the directory where Watchtower’s Docker client should find the certificate files within the Watchtower container. When it is unset, the Docker client loads no certificates from a directory. The examples on this page mount the certificates at /etc/ssl/docker and set this option to that path. Docker expects the following filenames: ca.pem cert.pem key.pem
data.tls-verification#TLS Verification:
Argument: --tlsverify Environment Variable: DOCKER_TLS_VERIFY Type: Boolean Default: false http:// and unix:// schemes are incompatible with TLS verification. When TLS verification is enabled
The use of tcp:// or https:// schemes for the Docker host URL is required. An https:// host is treated as tcp://, since the certificates, not the scheme, make the connection use TLS. The TLS certificate path is required for a remote host. Without it, Watchtower stops at startup rather than connect without TLS. Watchtower reads DOCKER_TLS_VERIFY as a boolean, so 0 or false turns verification off. The Docker CLI verifies when the variable has any value.
data.tutorial-overview#Tutorial Overview:
In order for Watchtower to connect via TLS to a Docker daemon, the Docker daemon must be setup to accept remote connections using TLS.
Setting up TLS for Docker involves several key steps:
Certificate Generation:
Create a Certificate Authority (CA), server certificate, and client certificates using OpenSSL or similar tools. Server certificates must include the Docker host’s IP or DNS name in the Subject Alternative Name (SAN) field. Daemon Configuration:
Start the Docker daemon with TLS options:
--tlsverify: Enable TLS verification --tlscacert: Path to CA certificate --tlscert: Path to server certificate --tlskey: Path to server private key Client Setup:
Prepare client certificates (cert.pem and key.pem) for authentication. Environment Variables:
Set DOCKER_HOST to the secure endpoint (e.g., tcp://docker.example.com:2376) Set DOCKER_CERT_PATH to the directory containing client certificates Set DOCKER_TLS_VERIFY=1 to enable verification For detailed instructions, refer to the Docker documentation on protecting the Docker daemon socket .
data.watchtower-configuration#Watchtower Conf:
Docker ComposeDocker CLI services: watchtower: image: nickfedor/watchtower environment: - DOCKER_HOST=tcp://HOST:2376 - DOCKER_CERT_PATH=/etc/ssl/docker - DOCKER_TLS_VERIFY=1 volumes: - CERT_DIR:/etc/ssl/docker:ro restart: unless-stopped docker run -d \ --name watchtower \ -v "CERT_DIR:/etc/ssl/docker:ro" \ nickfedor/watchtower --host tcp://HOST:2376 --cert-path /etc/ssl/docker --tlsverify Replace the following:
HOST: the host name or IP address of the Docker host, as named in its server certificate. Enclose an IPv6 address in brackets, such as [2001:db8::1]. CERT_DIR: the absolute path of a directory that holds only the client’s ca.pem, cert.pem and key.pem files. Do not use /etc/docker/certs, which also holds the CA and server private keys.

data:
When Watchtower detects that a running container needs to be updated it will stop the container by sending it a SIGTERM signal. If your container should be shutdown with a different signal you can communicate this to Watchtower by setting a label named com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.stop-signal with the value of the desired signal.
This label can be coded directly into your image by using the LABEL instruction in your Dockerfile:
LABEL com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.stop-signal="SIGHUP" Or, it can be specified as part of the docker run command line:
docker run -d --label=com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.stop-signal=SIGHUP someimage

Reference for Watchtower configuration options and behavior.
Introduction How configuration is applied Docker Connection Connect to the Docker engine Container Selection Filter monitored containers Scheduling Intervals, cron, and run-once Registry & Authentication Private registries and credentials Git Monitoring Git watcher options and credentials Image Cooldown Delay repeated image updates Update Behavior How containers are replaced Lifecycle Hooks Pre/post update commands Logging and Output Log levels and formats Notifications Notification-related options HTTP API Enable and configure the API

data.copy-files-during-recreate#Copy Files Du:
Copies named files from the old container into the replacement container during an update.
This is a per-container label, not a Watchtower process option. Set com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.copy-file to a comma-separated list of absolute paths inside the container.
Use this for Docker Compose configs that use content: or environment:. Compose file: configs are bind-mounts and are already preserved.
See Copy Files for path rules and Compose examples.
data.disable-containers-by-label#Disable Cont:
Excludes containers that have any of the specified label key-value pairs from monitoring.
Argument: --disable-containers-by-label Environment Variable: WATCHTOWER_DISABLE_CONTAINERS_BY_LABEL Type: Comma-separated list of key=value pairs Default: None Values containing commas are not supported. Use individual key=value pairs separated by commas. A label entry with an empty value (key=) performs a presence check: the label must exist on the container with any value. A non-empty value requires an exact match. A key can be listed more than once, as in env=dev,env=test. A container is then excluded when its label has any of those values. Dependencies on excluded containers are ignored. See Dependencies on Unmonitored Containers.
data.disable-specific-containers#Disable Spec:
Excludes containers by container name from monitoring, even if they have the enable label set to true.
Argument: --disable-containers, -x Environment Variable: WATCHTOWER_DISABLE_CONTAINERS Type: Comma- or space-separated string list Default: None Regex patterns are supported. See Regex Pattern Matching for details. Dependencies on excluded containers are ignored. See Dependencies on Unmonitored Containers.
data.enable-containers-by-label#Enable Contai:
Restricts monitoring to containers that have at least one of the specified label key-value pairs.
Argument: --enable-containers-by-label Environment Variable: WATCHTOWER_ENABLE_CONTAINERS_BY_LABEL Type: Comma-separated list of key=value pairs Default: None Values containing commas are not supported. Use individual key=value pairs separated by commas. A label entry with an empty value (key=) performs a presence check: the label must exist on the container with any value. A non-empty value requires an exact match. A key can be listed more than once, as in env=prod,env=staging. A container then matches when its label has any of those values. Dependencies on excluded containers are ignored. See Dependencies on Unmonitored Containers.
data.enable-label-filter#Enable Label Filter:
Restricts monitoring to containers with the com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.enable label set to true when the --label-enable flag is specified. Without --label-enable, containers with this label set to false are excluded, while others are monitored by default.
Argument: --label-enable Environment Variable: WATCHTOWER_LABEL_ENABLE Type: Boolean Default: false When --label-enable is unset, containers without the com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.enable label or with it set to true are monitored, and those with false are excluded.
When --label-enable is set, only containers with true are monitored, ignoring those with false or no label.
Dependencies on excluded containers are ignored. See Dependencies on Unmonitored Containers.
data.include-restarting-containers#Include Re:
Includes containers in the restarting state for monitoring and updates.
Argument: --include-restarting Environment Variable: WATCHTOWER_INCLUDE_RESTARTING Type: Boolean Default: false
data.include-stopped-containers#Include Stopp:

Argument: --include-stopped, -S Environment Variable: WATCHTOWER_INCLUDE_STOPPED Type: Boolean Default: false
data.label-precedence#Label Precedence:
Allows container labels (e.g., com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.monitor-only, com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.no-pull) to override corresponding flags.
Argument: --label-take-precedence Environment Variable: WATCHTOWER_LABEL_TAKE_PRECEDENCE Type: Boolean Default: false
data.monitor-specific-images#Monitor Specific:
Restricts monitoring to containers whose image name matches one of the supplied image name patterns, even if other selection criteria would include them.
Argument: --monitor-image-names Environment Variable: WATCHTOWER_MONITOR_IMAGE_NAMES Type: Comma or space-separated string list Default: None Image name patterns include the tag (for example nginx:latest). Regex patterns are supported and anchored to the full image name. See Regex Pattern Matching for details. Dependencies on excluded containers are ignored. See Dependencies on Unmonitored Containers.
data.revive-stopped-containers#Revive Stopped:
Restarts stopped containers after their images are updated.
Argument: --revive-stopped Environment Variable: WATCHTOWER_REVIVE_STOPPED Type: Boolean Default: false Requires --include-stopped.
data.scope-filter#Scope Filter:
Monitors containers with a com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.scope label matching the specified value, enabling multiple Watchtower instances.
Argument: --scope Environment Variable: WATCHTOWER_SCOPE Type: String Default: None Set to none to ignore scoped containers. Without this option, Watchtower takes its scope from the com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.scope label of its own container. Without that label either, it monitors only containers without a scope, as with none.
For self-updates, ensure all Watchtower containers share the same com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.scope label to guarantee cleanup of renamed containers and old images. Mismatched labels may prevent detection, leaving resources running.
See Running Multiple Instances.
Dependencies on excluded containers are ignored. See Dependencies on Unmonitored Containers.
data.skip-specific-images#Skip Specific Image:
Excludes containers by image name pattern from monitoring, even if they have the enable label set to true.
Argument: --skip-image-names Environment Variable: WATCHTOWER_SKIP_IMAGE_NAMES Type: Comma or space-separated string list Default: None Image name patterns include the tag (for example nginx:latest). Regex patterns are supported and anchored to the full image name. See Regex Pattern Matching for details. Dependencies on excluded containers are ignored. See Dependencies on Unmonitored Containers.
data.use-docker-compose-depends-on#Use Docker:
Enables or disables processing of the Docker Compose depends_on configuration for determining container update order.
Argument: --use-compose-depends-on Environment Variable: WATCHTOWER_USE_COMPOSE_DEPENDS_ON Type: Boolean Default: true By default, Watchtower automatically detects and respects Docker Compose service dependencies. When this feature is disabled, only the Watchtower depends-on label, Docker links, network mode, and volumes_from are used. Disabling this is useful when you want to prevent Watchtower from automatically using Docker Compose dependencies but still use explicit Watchtower labels or Docker links for ordering. For more information on Watchtower’s handling of linked containers, please reference the Linked Containers documentation. Rolling restarts are not supported when any container has linked dependencies (including Docker Compose depends_on, Watchtower depends-on labels, Docker links, network mode, or volumes_from dependencies). When rolling-restart is enabled, the use-compose-depends-on configuration option controls whether Docker Compose depends_on labels are included in the dependency validation check.

data.cpu-copy-mode#CPU Copy Mode:
Controls how CPU settings are copied when recreating containers, addressing Podman compatibility issues with CPU limits. Podman handles NanoCPUs differently than Docker, which can cause container recreation failures.
Argument: --cpu-copy-mode Environment Variable: WATCHTOWER_CPU_COPY_MODE Type: String Possible Values: auto, full, none Default: auto auto: Automatically detects if running on Podman and filters NanoCPUs for compatibility. On Docker, copies all CPU settings. full: Copies all CPU settings unchanged (original behavior). none: Strips all CPU limits to avoid compatibility issues. Use auto in mixed Docker/Podman environments. Use full if running only on Docker and want to preserve all CPU limits. Use none if CPU limits are causing issues and you prefer no limits on recreated containers.
data.disable-memory-swappiness#Disable Memory:
Sets memory swappiness to nil for Podman compatibility with crun and cgroupv2, overriding Podman’s default of 0.
Argument: --disable-memory-swappiness Environment Variable: WATCHTOWER_DISABLE_MEMORY_SWAPPINESS Type: Boolean Default: false
data.docker-api-version#Docker API Version:
Sets the Docker API version for client-daemon communication.
Argument: --api-version, -a Environment Variable: DOCKER_API_VERSION Type: String Default: Autonegotiated Falls back to autonegotiation on failure. Refer to Docker’s API version matrix for compatibility.
data.docker-host#Docker Host:
Specifies the Docker daemon socket to connect to, supporting remote hosts via TCP (e.g., tcp://hostname:port).
Argument: --host, -H Environment Variable: DOCKER_HOST Type: String Default: unix:///var/run/docker.sock
data.enable-docker-tls-verification#Enable Do:
Enables TLS verification for Docker socket connections.
Argument: --tlsverify Environment Variable: DOCKER_TLS_VERIFY Type: Boolean Default: false
data.recreating-containers-on-podman#Recreati:
Watchtower talks to Podman through its Docker-compatible API. It recreates a container from what that API reports. A setting the API does not carry is lost on recreation.
Timezone and umask: Podman’s --tz and --umask exist only in Podman’s own API. A recreated container uses the image’s timezone. Its processes run with the OCI runtime’s default umask, normally 0022. Log driver: the Docker-compatible API reports a k8s-file log driver as json-file and leaves out its options, such as max-size. A recreated container uses json-file without those options. Its log size limit falls back to log_size_max in containers.conf, which is unlimited by default. Podman metadata: fields such as CreateCommand and the systemd notify mode are not part of the Docker API. A recreated container does not have them. To keep these settings, set them where Watchtower does not need to copy them. For example, set the timezone through the TZ environment variable. Watchtower keeps the variable on recreation. It takes effect when the image or application reads it. Or manage the container with a Podman Quadlet or systemd unit and let Podman’s own auto-update restart it.
data.tls-certificates-path#TLS Certificates P:
Path to TLS certificates for remote Docker connections.
Argument: --cert-path Environment Variable: DOCKER_CERT_PATH Type: String Default: None
data.usage-examples#Usage Examples:
Run Watchtower with automatic CPU compatibility:
docker run -d \ --name watchtower \ -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \ nickfedor/watchtower \ --cpu-copy-mode auto Force full CPU copying (Docker-only environments):
docker run -d \ --name watchtower \ -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \ nickfedor/watchtower \ --cpu-copy-mode full Strip all CPU limits:
docker run -d \ --name watchtower \ -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \ nickfedor/watchtower \ --cpu-copy-mode none

data.git-ca-bundle#Git CA Bundle:
Path to a PEM file of extra CA certificates for Git HTTPS. Applied to clone, ls-remote, REST probes, and local path project checkout.

Save local files in a Compose project directory, check out the monitored commit, then write those files back. Use this when the project has local files that are not gitignored, such as an extra .env. data.git-context#Git Context:
Default subdirectory of a Git URL context sent to the Docker daemon as the build context. Used when a container does not set com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.git-context. Empty means the repository root.

data.git-image#Git Image:
Associates an image name with a Git repository. Repeatable. Not comma-glued. Format: image=repo[#ref][@policy].

data.git-insecure-skip-tls#Git Insecure Skip:
Skip TLS verification for Git HTTPS. Applied to clone, ls-remote, REST probes, and local path project checkout.

data.git-password#Git Password:
Basic-auth password for private repositories.
Argument: --git-password Environment Variable: WATCHTOWER_GIT_PASSWORD Type: String Default: (empty) Supports a file path for Docker Secrets (for example /run/secrets/git_password). Prefer Docker Secrets over putting the password in the environment. Passwords never appear in labels, /v1/config, or events.
data.git-ssh-key-path#Git SSH Key Path:

Step Limit Check a hosted ref for a new commit Git timeout Check out a local path context Git timeout Build an image from a Git URL context, including the daemon’s clone 30 minutes Apply a Compose project 30 minutes Builds and Compose applies run Dockerfile steps that can take minutes, so the Git timeout does not limit them.

Comma-separated list of allowed CORS origins for cross-origin requests. Use this to restrict which origins can access the API.
Argument: --http-api-cors-origins Environment Variable: WATCHTOWER_HTTP_API_CORS_ORIGINS Type: String Array Default: Unset (same-origin only) When unset, CORS is disabled and only same-origin requests are allowed. Set this to permit specific cross-origin origins.
data.http-api-endpoints#HTTP API Endpoints:
Selects which HTTP API endpoints to enable.
Argument: --http-api-endpoints Environment Variable: WATCHTOWER_HTTP_API_ENDPOINTS Type: String (comma or whitespace separated list) Default: empty (HTTP API disabled) For more information, review the HTTP API documentation Valid names (case-insensitive):
Name Routes Auth health /livez, /readyz, /startupz None update POST /v1/update http-api-token metrics GET /v1/metrics, GET /v1/status http-api-token containers GET /v1/containers, /v1/containers/details http-api-token check POST /v1/check http-api-token history GET /v1/history http-api-token images GET /v1/images http-api-token config GET /v1/config http-api-token events GET /v1/events http-api-events-token swagger GET /swagger/* None Protected /v1/* endpoints require configuring a http-api-token. Enabling events requires configuring a http-api-events-token. The all value enables every endpoint and MUST be the only value. Watchtower will exit on startup if an incorrect name is used or combined with all. Flag and environment value usage
The CLI flag can be specified multiple times. Defining the environment variable multiple times will not work (only the last value is used). For environment variables use comma or space-separated values.
data.http-api-events-token#HTTP API Events To:
Sets an authentication token with read-only permissions specifically for the events SSE endpoint (/v1/events).
Argument: --http-api-events-token Environment Variable: WATCHTOWER_HTTP_API_EVENTS_TOKEN Type: String Default: None This is a separate token from the http-api-token in order to reduce credential exposure, because events tokens may be exposed in URL query parameters.
The token can be provided via the Authorization header (for programmatic clients) or as the access_token query parameter (for browser EventSource which cannot set custom headers).
Events token leakage risk
When using the access_token query parameter (required for browser EventSource), the token appears in browser history, proxy logs, and access logs. This is a lower exposure than the main API token, but you should still treat the events token as a secret and rotate it if it has been exposed. Prefer header-based auth when possible.
This is required when the events endpoint is enabled via http-api-endpoints. Supports file path for Docker Secrets (e.g., /run/secrets/http_api_events_token).
data.http-api-host#HTTP API Host:

data.cooldown-delay#Cooldown Delay:
Sets a global minimum image age before Watchtower will perform the update.
Image age is determined from the image creation timestamp in the registry config blob. This helps to establish a time buffer against newly pushed images; however, is not a comprehensive security control.
Argument: --cooldown-delay Environment Variable: WATCHTOWER_COOLDOWN_DELAY Type: String Default: (empty / disabled) Accepted units: h (hours), m (minutes), s (seconds), d (days), w (weeks), M (months, i.e. 30 days). These can be combined (e.g., 24h, 3d, 1w, 1M, 1w12h). Leaving the setting empty disables cooldown. This setting delays all updates, including critical security patches. Operators should weigh the trade-off between update immediacy and exposure to unverified images. See Image Cooldown for detailed information on how cooldown works, boundary behavior, per-container labels, limitations, and interaction with other features like --no-pull.
data.cooldown-platform-architecture#Cooldown:
Overrides the architecture used for platform selection when fetching image manifests during cooldown checks. By default, Watchtower uses the runtime architecture (e.g., amd64, arm64).
Argument: None Environment Variable: WATCHTOWER_COOLDOWN_PLATFORM_ARCH Type: String Default: runtime.GOARCH Useful for cross-platform monitoring (e.g., monitoring arm64 containers from an amd64 host). Only affects the cooldown image age check; does not impact Docker’s local platform detection.
See Image Cooldown for details on how platform selection works with multi-platform images.
data.cooldown-platform-os#Cooldown Platform O:
Overrides the OS used for platform selection when fetching image manifests during cooldown checks. By default, Watchtower uses the runtime OS (e.g., linux).
Argument: None Environment Variable: WATCHTOWER_COOLDOWN_PLATFORM_OS Type: String Default: runtime.GOOS Useful for cross-platform monitoring (e.g., monitoring Linux containers from a macOS or Windows host). Only affects the cooldown image age check; does not impact Docker’s local platform detection.
See Image Cooldown for details on how platform selection works with multi-platform images.
data.cooldown-platform-variant#Cooldown Platf:
Specifies the platform variant for platform selection when fetching image manifests during cooldown checks. This disambiguates when multiple image index entries share the same OS and architecture but differ by variant (e.g., ARM v7 vs v8).
Argument: None Environment Variable: WATCHTOWER_COOLDOWN_PLATFORM_VARIANT Type: String Default: None Required only for ARM images with multiple variants (e.g., v7, v8). When not specified and multiple variants exist, Watchtower returns an ambiguous platform match error.
See Image Cooldown for details on how platform selection works with multi-platform images.

data.health-check#Health Check:

data.health-check-with-podman#Health Check wi:
Podman ignores the HEALTHCHECK instruction in the Watchtower image. The image is published in the OCI format, and Podman only reads health checks from images in the Docker format (containers/podman#18904 ). To enable the health check under Podman, define it in your container configuration, as shown below.
Docker ComposePodman CLIQuadlet services: watchtower: image: nickfedor/watchtower:latest healthcheck: test: ["CMD", "/watchtower", "--health-check"] volumes: - /run/podman/podman.sock:/var/run/docker.sock podman run -d \ --name watchtower \ --health-cmd '["/watchtower", "--health-check"]' \ -v /run/podman/podman.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \ nickfedor/watchtower [Container] Image=docker.io/nickfedor/watchtower:latest HealthCmd=["/watchtower", "--health-check"] Volume=/run/podman/podman.sock:/var/run/docker.sock Use the exec form shown above. Because the image does not include a shell, a shell-form health check, such as --health-cmd "/watchtower --health-check" or a CMD-SHELL test, always reports the container as unhealthy. Docker Compose requires CMD as the first entry of the test list. Without it, Compose fails with the error healthcheck.test must start either by "CMD", "CMD-SHELL" or "NONE". For rootless Podman, mount the socket from $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/podman/podman.sock instead of /run/podman/podman.sock.
data.help#Help:
Displays documentation for supported flags.
Argument: --help Environment Variable: N/A Type: N/A Default: N/A
data.overview#Overview:
By default, Watchtower monitors all containers running on the Docker daemon it connects to (typically the local daemon, configurable via the --host flag).
To limit monitoring to specific containers, provide their names as arguments when starting Watchtower.
Docker ComposeDocker CLI services: watchtower: command: nginx redis image: nickfedor/watchtower:latest volumes: - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock docker run -d \ --name watchtower \ -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \ --restart unless-stopped \ nickfedor/watchtower \ nginx redis In the above example, Watchtower monitors only the nginx and redis containers, ignoring others. To run a single update attempt and exit, use the run-once configuration option.
Docker ComposeDocker CLI services: watchtower: command: nginx redis environment: WATCHTOWER_RUN_ONCE: true image: nickfedor/watchtower:latest volumes: - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock docker run --rm \ -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \ nickfedor/watchtower \ --run-once \ nginx redis This command triggers an update attempt for “nginx” and “redis” containers, displays debug output, and removes the Watchtower container upon completion. By default, Watchtower decides that an image is stale by comparing registry digests. Git monitoring is an optional alternate staleness signal: associate a container with a hosted repository, and Watchtower rebuilds from a Git URL context or a local Compose project directory when that ref changes. See Advanced Features → Git Monitoring.
Regex patterns are supported. See Regex Pattern Matching for details. Startup errors
When a configuration option or flag is invalid, Watchtower exits at startup.
In a container, Watchtower first sets its restart policy to no, so the container does not restart in a loop. Start the container again once the configuration is fixed. A --host flag after an invalid flag is not read. Watchtower then connects through DOCKER_HOST or the default socket. If Watchtower cannot change its restart policy, it logs an error.

data.enable-lifecycle-hooks#Enable Lifecycle:

data.lifecycle-uid#Lifecycle UID:
Sets the default user ID to run lifecycle hooks as when no container-specific UID is specified. The value must be from 0 to 2147483647, the highest ID the container runtime accepts. Watchtower exits at startup if it is outside that range.
Argument: --lifecycle-uid Environment Variable: WATCHTOWER_LIFECYCLE_UID Type: Integer Default: None Container-specific labels (com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.lifecycle.uid) take precedence over this global setting.
